trajectory_summary: The call opens neutrally and briefly warms when the customer volunteers detailed bill history and explicit willingness to keep listening, but the rep never asks why he's interested in solar, never captures or uses the bill figures he offers, and unilaterally disqualifies him over shading in under two minutes. The call ends with the rep closing the file rather than routing to a closer or logging the lead for reassessment.
outcome_dispute: This should be tagged dq, not a soft no-appointment — the rep explicitly disqualifies the lead ('I can just remove you from my list') on her own read of sun exposure, which is a closer/design-tier judgment the setter is not positioned to make from a phone call alone.

observed_outcome.quote: yeah, like you said, you're not open to removing the trees at all, so solar won't work for you. I can just remove you from my list.
observed_outcome.reasoning: The rep explicitly disqualifies the lead and offers to remove him from her list; no appointment, tentative time, or callback was set — the call ends on the rep's own DQ determination.

bill_anchor_audit.bill_quote: the highest bill I've ever had was a $109. And my average bill, I'd say, over a course of twelve months is around 76 to $81.
bill_anchor_audit.reasoning: The customer volunteered specific bill figures unprompted, but the rep never acknowledged the number or used it in any direction (flip or otherwise) — the conversation immediately moved to the shading/DQ track instead.

interest_reason_audit.reasoning: The rep never explicitly asked what interested Kevin in solar; the call moved from address/homeowner verification straight into the shading concern and then to bill discussion the customer volunteered, without a direct interest question ever being asked.

primary_coaching_focus.topic: unilateral DQ on unverified shading assessment
primary_coaching_focus.quote: so solar won't work for you. I can just remove you from my list.
primary_coaching_focus.why: The rep made a design-tier technical call (insufficient sun exposure) with no imagery or tool reference and closed the lead within two minutes of raising it, on a customer who explicitly said he was 'more willing to listen.' This is the costliest single moment on the call — a real lead with detailed bill data and stated openness was let go on a guess.

key_moments.quote: one thing I'm a little concerned about is you've got some trees that are putting some shade on the home.
key_moments.stewart_read: Rep opens with a disqualifying frame instead of curiosity or qualification. This primes the whole call toward exit rather than toward building interest in seeing a design.

key_moments.quote: the highest bill I've ever had was a $109. And my average bill, I'd say, over a course of twelve months is around 76 to $81.
key_moments.stewart_read: Customer volunteers detailed bill figures unprompted — a rare gift of real usage data. Rep never acknowledges or reflects the number back, flipped or otherwise.

key_moments.quote: I've dealt with solar, like, quite a bit. So I don't I don't I mean, regardless of their incentives or not, it's just I don't think it can be done. But, I mean, I'm more willing to listen.
key_moments.stewart_read: Customer discloses significant prior solar experience/quotes ('breakeven over twenty one years... used to be a thirty six year payback') and explicit openness to continue. Rep never asks who he talked to, what was quoted, or what changed his numbers — competitive intel left on the table.

key_moments.quote: I think where where the situation is, where I'm at, right, is your home doesn't get enough sun exposure for a system to even work effectively.
key_moments.stewart_read: Rep makes a technical design determination (sun exposure sufficiency) that belongs to the design/closer team using satellite and shading tools, not a setter's phone judgment.
